name: subclass-sandbox
intent: Define each behaviour in its own subclass out of the operations its base class provides, so the whole family reaches the rest of the system through one base class instead of each sibling coupling to the engine on its own.
problem: A wide family of sibling classes - enemy abilities, hosted services, controller actions, stream implementations, test cases - all has to touch the same subsystem (physics, audio, particles, the request context), and each sibling is written by a different person. Left alone, every one of them pulls in the subsystem's headers or internals, repeats the same few calls, and the subsystem loses the ability to enforce rules that must hold for all of them. The catalog trigger: subclasses should compose behaviour only from base primitives.
context: Applies where one runtime is shared by a wide, shallow family of classes - game engine ability/entity hierarchies above all, but equally framework extension points written by application developers (request-handler bases, view/controller bases, stream bases, test-case bases) - and where the base class can realistically provide every operation a subclass may need, hiding subsystems whose internals are not a public API.
benefits: Each behaviour is coupled to one class instead of to the whole engine: a subclass file needs its base class and nothing else, so refactorings inside the engine stop rippling through dozens of siblings.

Duplication is rolled up: three abilities that each played a sound and spawned particles become three calls to shared, higher-level provided operations, and the next change to the audio API is applied once.

Invariants that must hold for every behaviour - audio queueing and prioritisation, permission checks, audit logging, rate limiting - live inside the primitives, where one implementation covers the whole family instead of a rule documented in a wiki.
Extending is additive: a new behaviour is a new subclass overriding one method, with no edit to the engine and no edit to the existing siblings (open/closed).
The primitive set documents the legal vocabulary: a reviewer can check that a behaviour composes only sanctioned operations, and a new author knows where work is supposed to start.

The hierarchy stays shallow and wide: one point of leverage where an improvement to the base benefits every subclass, and no deep chains in which an intermediate class can invalidate behaviour two levels down.
tradeoffs: Brittle base class: the base is now coupled to every subsystem any sibling touches, so changing a primitive's signature or semantics breaks many subclasses at once, and only the call sites the compiler can see are checked.

Base-class accretion: the pattern's own incentive - roll any duplicated code up into a shared operation - turns the base into a growing god object; once it is 'a bowl of code stew' it is the hardest class in the codebase to change.

Coupling is concentrated, not removed: N clean subclasses are bought with one over-coupled base class, so the pattern only pays off when the family is genuinely large and the behaviour genuinely overlaps.

The primitive set is a hard ceiling for behaviour authors: a behaviour that needs an operation the base does not provide must either edit the base (affecting every sibling at once) or reach around it into the engine, which voids the isolation the pattern was introduced for - and neither option is visible to the type checker.

The base's state has to come from somewhere, and every option costs something: constructor pass-through forces every derived constructor to forward the state, two-stage initialisation can leave half-built behaviours unless it is wrapped in a factory, and static state or a service locator hides global mutable dependencies that make behaviours harder to test and reason about.

The wall is a convention as much as a language feature: 'call only the provided operations' is enforced by an access modifier, a package boundary or a review rule, and one subclass that imports the engine directly breaks the isolation for exactly the case it was introduced to protect.

A class per behaviour does not fit behaviour that is really data: a freeze ray, a heat ray and a mustard ray differing only in numbers become three classes and a combinatorial family, where a table (Type Object, bytecode) would express the same thing without a subclass count that grows with content.

participants.responsibility: Declares the sandbox method and the provided operations, owns the coupling to the subsystems those operations drive, and keeps its state private so subclasses can reach it only through primitives.

The abstract (protected) operation every subclass must implement; it carries the behaviour's control flow and is the only place a subclass's own logic lives - in a game loop it is usually the update method.
The protected, normally non-virtual operations implemented on the base in terms of one or more subsystems; they are the sanctioned vocabulary and the place where family-wide invariants are enforced.
Implements the sandbox method by composing the provided operations only; it contributes behaviour, not engine access, and owns no knowledge of the subsystems behind the primitives.
A class that takes over a cluster of provided operations (audio, particles) when the base grows; the base exposes it through a single protected accessor so the primitive count stays readable.

use_cases: Game entity abilities: a hundred power classes that each override activate() while the base provides playSound, spawnParticles, move and the accessors for the hero's position - the pattern's originating scenario.
Engine update loops: entity types whose update() is the sandbox method, composing movement, animation and AI primitives that the base owns and every frame reuses (the Update Method overlap).

Framework extension bases: subclasses that compose documented primitives instead of internals - a Python request handler composing send_response/send_header/end_headers from do_GET, an ASP.NET Core controller composing Ok()/NotFound()/User from ControllerBase, a JDK list implementation maintaining the protected modCount from AbstractList.

Stream and protocol implementations where the subclass supplies one internal method and the base offers the buffering, state and callback plumbing as protected operations - Node.js stream implementations extend stream.Readable/Writable/Transform and must supply only _read/_write, while the base class owns push(), buffering and the event plumbing and documents the internal methods as not-to-be-called directly.
Plugin and SDK extension points where third-party code must be able to add behaviour without being handed the host's subsystems.
Test and assertion frameworks: test-case subclasses compose assertion primitives (assertEqual, assertRaises) instead of throwing and formatting failures themselves.

Component scripting in shipped engines: Unity MonoBehaviour subclasses implement lifecycle hooks (Start, Update) and compose engine primitives (GetComponent, Instantiate, StartCoroutine, Destroy) - the base forbids constructors so the host owns initialisation; Unreal Engine AActor subclasses override BeginPlay, Tick and EndPlay while the engine's documented actor lifecycle drives them and SpawnActor/Destroy stay the sanctioned spawn and teardown route.

Servlet containers: Jakarta HttpServlet requires a subclass to override at least one of doGet/doPost/doPut/doDelete, dispatches them from the base's service(), and hands the subclass the shared vocabulary of protected operations (getInitParameter, log, getServletConfig) instead of the container's request plumbing.
avoid_when: Only a handful of classes inherit and little behaviour is shared: a protected or private helper method, or a module of free functions, is simpler and has no base class to become brittle.
The variation is data rather than code (damage values, element types, level tables): use Type Object, a bytecode/data definition or a component-plus-data design instead of a subclass per row.
The behaviour must be chosen, replaced or combined per object at run time: composition (a component, strategy or delegate) beats a class per behaviour, which is fixed at definition time.

Most behaviours need operations the base cannot foresee, or the subsystem is already a stable, well-designed API: let the classes call it directly rather than routing every call through a sandbox that only forwards.

The family is extended by parties you do not control and the base changes often: a narrow non-virtual interface or an extension interface keeps compatibility, at the price of the shared primitive set.
Behaviours vary along two independent axes: one base class can only cover one axis, so a component/ECS decomposition fits better than a hierarchy of combinations.
anti_patterns: Public sandbox: the primitives are provided as ordinary public methods 'so everyone can use them', which turns the base into a general facade, drops the statement that they exist for subclasses, and lets unrelated callers depend on operations that were meant to be an internal vocabulary.

Pass-through primitives that add nothing: a provided operation that merely forwards to one engine call, hides no state, protects no invariant and removes no duplication - the base grows while the subclasses learn nothing.
Code stew: every helper any subclass ever wanted ends up flattened into the same base class until it is the largest, most coupled and least testable type in the project.

Deep hierarchy: behaviour subclasses of behaviour subclasses (Power -> FirePower -> Fireball), so a change to an intermediate class threatens a whole chain; the pattern prescribes a wide, shallow tree.

Reaching around the sandbox: a subclass imports the physics, audio or rendering API directly because the primitive it wanted does not exist - the centralised coupling comes back piecemeal and the base's invariants are bypassed.
Subclass per parameter: one class per element, level, damage value or configuration row, producing a combinatorial family where a data-driven definition belongs.
design_principles: Facade and information hiding: the base presents a simplified API over several subsystems and keeps their internals out of the subclass's file (Nystrom's single #include rule of thumb).
Separation of concerns: what a behaviour does is separated from how audio, physics or particles are driven.
DRY applied to the family: shared sequences of subsystem calls are lifted into named provided operations as soon as they repeat.
Open/closed principle: new behaviour arrives as a new subclass, while the engine and the existing siblings stay closed for modification.
Narrow interface / least knowledge: a subclass knows the base's vocabulary and nothing else about the system it runs in.
Single point of enforcement for cross-cutting rules (queueing, permissions, logging) - the sandbox's answer to aspect-like concerns.
best_practices: Mark the primitive API protected, and keep the primitives non-virtual wherever the language allows it, so subclasses can call the vocabulary but not redefine it.
Roll duplication up only when it pays: a primitive used by one exotic subclass adds complexity for everyone, so that subclass may call the subsystem directly while the base stays small.

Provide operations at the highest useful level (playSound(sound, volume) rather than play/stop/setVolume on the base), and move a growing cluster into a collaborator object reached through one protected accessor.
Keep the hierarchy wide and shallow: a behaviour hangs directly off the base, never off another behaviour.

Choose and document how the base gets its state - constructor pass-through, factory-wrapped two-stage init, static state, or a locator - and prefer constructor injection so a behaviour cannot exist half-built.
Keep invariants inside the primitives and state in the base's private fields; never hand out raw engine handles through a protected field.
Reconsider a data-driven definition (Type Object, bytecode, a table) once the family grows to dozens of near-identical classes, and keep the sandbox for behaviours with real control flow.
sources: Nystrom, Game Programming Patterns (Genever Benning, 2014) - Subclass Sandbox, Behavioral Patterns chapter: intent, sandbox method, provided operations, the brittle-base-class discussion and the design decisions on what to provide and how the base gets its state.
https://java-design-patterns.com/patterns/subclass-sandbox/ - same pattern described for Java, where it is also known as Hook Method.

https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/class-MonoBehaviour.html - Unity's own base class for gameplay scripts: lifecycle hooks (Start/Update) as the sandbox methods, engine helpers as the provided operations, and an explicit ban on constructors because the host owns instantiation.

https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/unreal-engine-actor-lifecycle - Unreal Engine's documented Actor lifecycle: the engine drives BeginPlay/Tick/EndPlay overrides and SpawnActor/Destroy are the sanctioned spawn and teardown operations.

https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html - Node.js streams API for implementors: subclasses supply the internal _read/_write while the base class owns push(), buffering and event plumbing, and the internal methods are documented as not to be called directly.

https://tomcat.apache.org/tomcat-11.0-doc/servletapi/jakarta/servlet/http/HttpServlet.html - Jakarta Servlet 6.1 API: a subclass must override at least one of doGet/doPost/doPut/doDelete, dispatched by the base's service(), with protected operations as the shared vocabulary.

https://kindatechnical.com/object-oriented-programming/fragile-base-class-problem.html - criticism of the inheritance-heavy design this pattern leans on: why deep hierarchies are risky and when to seal a base class against extension.
